      "checker_path": "none",
      "claim": "If the 2-factor routine reports that none exists, returning (G,nil) is correct.",

      "evidence": "Every Hamiltonian cycle is a spanning 2-regular subgraph, hence a 2-factor. Therefore a graph without a 2-factor is non-Hamiltonian. Returning the unchanged graph has edit distance zero, and nil is correct.",

      "claim": "If G has a 2-factor with q cycle components, one can add at most q edges and explicitly obtain a Hamiltonian cycle; if G is connected, at most q−1 additions suffice.",

The deleted edges are removed only from the cycle witness, not from G.",

    {
      "checker_path": "none",
      "claim": "For arbitrary fixed c>0, the target is polynomially solvable on graphs whose girth is at least c.",
      "claim_sha256": "35f2c323032497f7c3d546c609b200559e6762dcf0831f45552968ec2310b841",
      "evidence": "On the promised class, disconnected graphs and graphs without a 2-factor admit the preceding correct nil outputs. If a 2-factor exists and the girth is g≥c, each of its q cycles contains at least g vertices. Hence qg≤n and q≤n/g≤n/c. The general q-connector splice is therefore within the radius and constructs a Hamiltonian cycle. Forests cause no exception because they have no 2-factor.",

      "search_method": "Verified the promise interpretation, including acyclic graphs, and derived the component bound from cycle lengths.",

      "witness": "A computed 2-factor supplies cycles of length at least the promised girth; their endpoint connectors supply the output cycle."

      "evidence": "Given the stated S and partition, deleting all cross-part edges makes H−S have at least p components. If S is empty, p>1 makes H disconnected. If |S|=k>0, removing S from any spanning cycle leaves at most k path components; since that cycle would be a spanning subgraph of H−S, H−S could have at most k components. The condition p>k contradicts Hamiltonicity. Thus whenever the specified deletion set has size at most n/c, it gives a valid nil output within the radius.",

          "body_md": "## Object\n\nThe verified witness, as recorded by the blind-search stage:\n\nCleanest witness (distinct vertices, bipartite parity obstruction): the path graph P_3 on n = 3 vertices, V = {0,1,2}, E = {(0,1),(1,2)}.\n\nA =\n [0 1 0]\n [1 0 1]\n [0 1 0]\n\nA^(n-1) = A^2 =\n [1 0 1]\n [0 2 0]\n [1 0 1]\n\nThe graph is CONNECTED (verified by an independent BFS, not by the matrix). Yet A^2_{0,1} = 0, even though vertices 0 and 1 are ADJACENT — the explicit path 0->1 has length 1. Likewise A^2_{1,0} = A^2_{1,2} = A^2_{2,1} = 0. The claim says \"connected ==> A^(n-1)_{i,j} >= 1 for all i,j\"; here A^(n-1)_{0,1} = 0 < 1 in a connected graph, and the proof's inference \"A^{n-1}_{i,j}=0 ==> no path connecting i and j ==> graph disconnected\" is directly contradicted.\n\nEven smaller witness (diagonal entry): n = 2, K_2 with E = {(0,1)}. A^(n-1) = A^1 = [[0,1],[1,0]], so A^1_{0,0} = 0 while the graph is connected.\n\nMechanism, confirmed by the script's independent BFS 2-coloring: both witnesses are bipartite. A^k counts walks of length EXACTLY k; in a bipartite graph every i--j walk has a fixed length parity (equal to the parity of dist(i,j)), so walks of length exactly n-1 can be entirely absent between two vertices that are nevertheless joined by a path. Exhaustive check over all 2^0 = 1 edge subsets of the component C = ({2}, {}): the only choice is the empty red set, giving vertex 2 red degree 0, which is EVEN. Claim says: every node of C has odd red degree; here the only achievable red degree of vertex 2 is 0, and 0 is not odd. The same holds for {3}. Hence the resulting \"pave all red edges\" coloring gives vertices 2 and 3 red degree 0 (even) — the construction does not produce the required object.\n\nThis is a STRONG witness: it fails for EVERY choice of leaf (by symmetry all three leaves of K_{1,3} leave two singleton components), so the argument cannot be rescued by a cleverer leaf choice.\n\nNON-DEGENERATE WITNESS (bad component genuinely has edges, pre-empting the objection that only isolated vertices fail): T on 6 vertices with edges {(0,1),(0,2),(0,3),(1,4),(1,5)}; leaf A = 2, neighbour B = 0. Then F = T - A - B has the component C with vertices {1,4,5} and edges {(1,4),(1,5)}. The deletion rule only constrains the *remaining* degree (the number\nof still-present neighbors) at deletion time; it says nothing about the *back* degree\nto vertices that were deleted earlier. Those two quantities are unrelated, and the\nback degree can be arbitrarily larger than `t-1`.\n\n**Counterexample — the path `P₃`.**\nVertices `a = 0`, `b = 1`, `c = 2` with edges `ac = {0,2}` and `bc = {1,2}`\n(so `c` is the degree-`2` center; `a`, `b` are leaves).
